title: CHAPTER 8: MAJOR LANDFORMS OF THE EARTH

blocks.content: Landforms are the visible physical features of the Earth’s surface that have evolved over millions of years due to the combined action of internal (endogenic) and external (exogenic) forces.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Landforms are continuously shaped by internal forces (tectonic movements causing upliftment) and external forces (erosion and deposition).
Mountains are natural elevations categorized into Fold (e.g., Himalayas, Alps), Block (e.g., Vosges, Black Forest), and Volcanic (e.g., Mt. Kilimanjaro) types.
Plateaus are elevated flatlands or tablelands that serve as rich storehouses of mineral resources like iron, coal, and gold.
Plains are low-lying flat areas rarely exceeding 200 meters above sea level, mostly formed by river sediment deposition.
Plains are the most densely populated regions on Earth due to fertile soil, ease of transport, and suitability for agriculture.

blocks.content: Endogenic forces such as folding, faulting, volcanism, and plate tectonics build up the relief of the Earth, whereas exogenic forces such as weathering, erosion, transportation, and deposition continuously wear it down. The balance between these two sets of forces determines the present form of the Earth’s surface. For SSC examinations, this chapter is extremely scoring because it involves direct factual questions, conceptual questions, assertion–reason, and matching type MCQs.
Forces Responsible for Landform Development

Landforms are shaped by two major categories of forces. Endogenic forces originate within the Earth and are responsible for creating relief features. These include diastrophic movements such as folding and faulting, and sudden forces such as earthquakes and volcanoes. Exogenic forces operate on the Earth’s surface and include weathering, erosion, transportation, and deposition by agents like rivers, wind, glaciers, and sea waves.
Classification of Major Landforms

On the basis of elevation, slope, relative relief, and mode of formation, the Earth’s surface is broadly divided into three major landforms: Mountains, Plateaus, and Plains. These landforms occupy most of the Earth’s continental surface.
Mountains

Mountains are highly elevated landforms with steep slopes and narrow summits. They rise prominently above the surrounding areas and generally occur in long chains or ranges. Mountains are geologically unstable regions and are often associated with earthquakes, volcanic activity, and tectonic plate boundaries.
Mountain Building Processes (Orogenesis)

The process of mountain formation is known as orogenesis. Orogenesis mainly occurs due to compressional forces generated by plate movements. When plates collide, sedimentary rock layers are compressed, folded, or faulted, resulting in the formation of mountains.
Types of Mountains

Fold mountains are formed when sedimentary rock layers are subjected to intense compressional forces. Instead of breaking, the rock layers bend and fold. Fold mountains are usually very high, extensive, and young in geological age. They are characterized by anticlines and synclines.
Examples include the Himalayas (young fold mountains), the Alps, the Andes, and the Rockies.
Block mountains are formed due to faulting caused by tensional forces. When the Earth’s crust is stretched, it breaks into blocks. The uplifted blocks are called horsts and form block mountains,
while the downthrown blocks are called grabens and form rift valleys. Examples include the Black Forest and Vosges Mountains of Europe.

Volcanic mountains are formed by the accumulation of lava, ash, and other volcanic materials around volcanic vents during repeated eruptions. They are generally cone-shaped and may be active, dormant, or extinct. Examples include Mount Fuji (Japan), Mount Kilimanjaro (Africa), and Mount Vesuvius (Italy).
Landforms are shaped by continuous internal upliftment and external erosional processes on the surface of the Earth.

Residual mountains are formed as a result of prolonged erosion of ancient mountain ranges. Over time, erosion reduces the height of mountains, leaving behind hard rock masses. These mountains are very old and low in height. The Aravalli Range in India is one of the oldest examples of residual mountains.
Importance of Mountains

Mountains significantly influence climate by acting as barriers to winds and rainfall, resulting in orographic rainfall on windward slopes and rain shadow regions on leeward sides. They are the source of major rivers and glaciers and supply water for irrigation, drinking, and hydroelectric power generation. Mountains are rich in minerals, forests, and biodiversity, and also serve as natural political and cultural boundaries.
Plateaus

Plateaus are elevated flat or gently undulating landforms with steep sides. They are also known as tablelands and often represent old land surfaces. Plateaus cover extensive areas of the Earth and are economically significant.
Formation of Plateaus

Plateaus are formed due to tectonic uplift of large areas, extensive volcanic lava flows, or prolonged erosion of surrounding lowlands. In many cases, more than one process may be responsible for their formation.
Types of Plateaus

Intermontane plateaus are located between mountain ranges and are usually very high. They are formed when land between folded mountains is uplifted. The Tibetan Plateau, also known as the Roof of the World, is the highest and largest intermontane plateau.

blocks.content: Volcanic plateaus are formed by successive lava flows that spread over large areas and solidify into flat surfaces. The Deccan Plateau in India is a classic example formed by basaltic lava flows.
Dissected plateaus are formed when rivers and streams cut deep valleys into a plateau, creating rugged terrain. The Chota Nagpur Plateau of India is an example of a dissected plateau.
Importance of Plateaus

Plateaus are rich in mineral resources such as coal, iron ore, manganese, and bauxite. They are major centres of mining and industrial development. Plateaus are suitable for grazing and hydroelectric power generation.
Plains

Plains are extensive low-lying landforms with flat or gently sloping surfaces. They are mainly formed by the deposition of sediments carried by rivers, wind, glaciers, and sea waves. Plains are the most productive and densely populated regions of the world.
Formation of Plains

Plains are formed when eroded materials from mountains are transported by agents of erosion and deposited in low-lying areas over long periods. Repeated deposition creates thick layers of fertile alluvium.
Types of Plains
Structural plains are formed due to uplift or subsidence of land without much deformation. They have relatively simple geological structures.

items: In Block Mountains, uplifted blocks are called 'Horsts' and lowered blocks are called 'Graben' (e.g., Rhine Valley and Vosges mountain system).
The Tibetan Plateau is frequently tested as the highest plateau in the world, with an elevation of 4,000 to 6,000 meters above sea level.
Aravalli range in India is one of the oldest fold mountain systems in the world, now significantly worn down by erosion.

blocks.content: Erosional plains are formed by long-term erosion of elevated regions. The process removes irregularities and produces nearly level surfaces.
Depositional plains are formed by deposition of sediments by rivers, glaciers, wind, or sea waves. Alluvial plains formed by rivers are among the most fertile regions in the world.
Importance of Plains

Plains support intensive agriculture due to fertile soils and availability of water. They facilitate easy construction of transport networks and cities, making them centres of population and economic activities.
Overall Importance of Major Landforms

Major landforms control climate, drainage patterns, soil distribution, vegetation, human settlement, agriculture, industry, and transport. They are fundamental to understanding physical and human geography.
